opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest difference is how concentrated the focus becomes. As faculty, your attention is naturally spread across many things: you're advising students who each have their own projects and interests, teaching, writing grants, serving on committees, reviewing papers. A lot of the job is about cultivating people and letting a hundred flowers bloom. That diversity is really valuable, because some of the most interesting ideas come from a student wandering somewhere you'd never have pointed them.

At a startup, it's almost the opposite. You have to pick a direction and commit. The whole team is rowing toward one goal, and every week you're asking whether what you're doing actually moves that goal forward. There's much less room for "this is a cool side question, let's write a paper on it." That's sometimes painful for someone who grew up in research, because you see interesting threads and have to consciously let them go.

But there's something very energizing about it, too. In academia you often stop at the proof of concept: you show the idea works on a benchmark, publish it, and move on. In a startup you have to carry the idea all the way through, deal with scale, data, engineering, and whether it actually works for real users. That forces a kind of honesty about which ideas are fundamental and which only look good in a paper.

So I'd say academia optimizes for breadth and exploration, and a startup optimizes for depth and execution. I don't think one is better. Ideally you want both mindsets, and moving between them has made me appreciate what each one is good at.

r001.rationale: The response says faculty attention is spread across students, teaching, grants, and other duties, but does not identify managing multiple projects as causing context switching.

r002.rationale: It contrasts faculty breadth with startup work that requires picking a direction and committing the team to one goal.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I actually live in both worlds right now. I'm at NYU as faculty, and I also spend time on the startup side. The difference in focus is bigger than people expect.

In academia, the question that drives you is "what's interesting?" You pick a problem because nobody understands it yet, and you're allowed to spend a year or two on something that may never turn into a product. That freedom is the whole point. A lot of the work I'm proudest of, like ConvNeXt or diffusion transformers, started from a simple curiosity: can we take an old idea seriously again and see how far it goes? There was no deadline, no customer, no roadmap. Students are also a huge part of it. Half of what I do is help someone become an independent researcher, and that shapes which problems you choose. You want problems where a PhD student can own the whole thing and learn from it.

At a startup, the question is "what matters right now?" You have a product, you have compute constraints, you have users who will tell you very quickly if something doesn't work. The focus becomes much narrower and much deeper. You can't explore ten ideas. You pick one or two and push them extremely hard, because the clock is actually running. And the feedback loop is tighter. In academia, feedback comes at a conference six months later. At a startup, it comes the next morning.

What I find healthy is that each side corrects the other. Academia can drift into writing papers for other papers. The startup keeps pulling me back to ask whether this actually changes anything for a real system. And the startup can get tunnel vision, where you optimize the thing in front of you and forget to step back. The academic side keeps asking what the real underlying question is, and whether we're even measuring the right thing.

The hardest part honestly is context switching. The two modes use a different kind of attention. Research is wide and patient. A startup is narrow and urgent. You can't be both at the same moment, so I've had to be very deliberate about which hat I'm wearing on a given day.

r001.rationale: The response describes context switching between academic and startup modes, but does not identify managing multiple projects as a source of context switching for university faculty.

r002.rationale: It says startup work is narrower and deeper, with one or two ideas pushed hard, while contrasting this with academic freedom to explore.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is how you choose what to focus on. As faculty, you have a lot of freedom to ask, “What’s an interesting question? What could matter in the long run?” And part of your job is helping students develop their own judgment, so you’re supporting several different directions.

At a startup, you need a much tighter connection between the research and what you’re trying to build. There are lots of interesting problems, but the question is, “Which one is actually blocking us right now?” You have to make choices and get feedback quickly.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the research is less ambitious. It means the ambition has to be concentrated. In academia, exploring a new direction can itself be a valuable outcome. At a startup, you also need to turn that exploration into something that works.

r001.rationale: The response says faculty support several directions, but it does not identify managing multiple projects as causing context switching.

r002.rationale: It contrasts faculty’s several directions with startup work’s tighter connection to what is being built and says startup ambition must be concentrated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is how you choose what to focus on. As faculty, you have more freedom to explore a question because you find it interesting, even if you don’t know where it will lead. You’re also thinking about students and helping them develop their own research direction.

At a startup, you need a much tighter connection between the research and what the team is trying to build. There are many interesting problems, but you have to ask: Which one matters most right now? What will solving it actually unlock? So the focus becomes more concentrated, and the feedback loop is shorter. You still need curiosity, but you have to be very deliberate about where you spend it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses faculty freedom to explore and support students, but does not mention managing multiple projects or context switching.

r002.rationale: It says startup focus is more concentrated, but does not clearly state that startup work centers on a single undertaking compared with faculty work.
